concept.title: Dark Mathematics: Theorems That Exist But Cannot Be Found
concept.concept_description: There are mathematical objects whose existence we can prove but whose specific properties are unknowable — theorems that cast shadows without being visible. Define a dark theorem as a statement T such that: (1) PA proves 'there exists x such that T(x)', but (2) for every specific n, PA does NOT prove T(n). The classic example is the Paris-Harrington theorem: the strengthened finite Ramsey theorem is true but not provable in PA. But dark theorems go further: they assert the existence of objects that no specific instance can be verified. Conjecture: The set of dark theorems is dense in the space of all Pi_2 statements — most true Pi_2 statements are dark. Moreover, there is a hierarchy of darkness: a dark theorem of level k is one where PA proves 'there exist at least k values of x such that T(x)' but cannot identify any specific one. The hierarchy is strict: level k+1 dark theorems are strictly harder to prove than level k. Test: construct explicit dark theorems of levels 1, 2, 3 using the Paris-Harrington principle and the Kirby-Paris hydra theorem. Prove the density conjecture by counting Pi_2 statements. Impact: most true mathematical statements are dark — they assert existence without the possibility of verification. This is not incompleteness; it is a new form of mathematical unknowability.

Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X.
